transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-16 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~34 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (Velaris CTO), Maya Chen (ML Eng), Liam O'Neill (SRE)
---
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Jordan with Redwood Inference, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Tom (CTO): Good, thanks. We're excited to see the hosted API flow — we've been evaluating options for low-latency chat features.
[00:12] Priya (SE): Great, quick agenda: we'll do a quick overview of hosted API, jump into the console for a streaming demo, show some SDK examples (streaming + retries), then cover parameter tradeoffs and Q&A. Sound good?
[00:20] Maya (ML Eng): Yep, sounds great. We're particularly interested in streaming and how to tune params to meet latency and cost targets.
[00:26] Jordan: Perfect. I'll start with a 2-minute overview: Redwood's hosted API gives you text generation, chat, embeddings, reranking, etc. For hosted customers you get a curated model catalog and streaming responses out of the box. We also provide observability in the Console — token breakdowns and per-route latency.
[00:40] Tom: Quick Q: how do you handle retries if the model instance is busy or there's network flakiness? We need idempotent behavior for our user flows.
[00:48] Priya: Good Q. We recommend idempotency keys on requests. Our SDK has built-in retry helpers with exponential backoff and jitter; you can configure 429 vs 5xx policies separately. For streaming we buffer partial tokens locally and will resume or restart depending on where failure happened — there's a short note in the docs, I can share the exact code snippet.
[01:06] Jordan: I'll flag that for action item — Priya will share the notebook.
[01:10] Priya: Okay jumping into the Console — I'm sharing my screen. You might see some intermittent caption errors in the transcript, apologies.
[01:18] [01:18] Priya (SE): Here in the Console, we have a playground for chat. I'm toggling streaming on — when enabled, the API streams tokens as they're generated rather than waiting for the full response. That reduces perceived latency for the user.
[01:35] Priya: Example settings: temperature (0.0-1.0), top_p, max_tokens, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty. Lower temperature yields more deterministic output; higher temperature increases diversity. Also note cost is proportional to generated tokens, so max_tokens is an important control.
[01:55] Maya: For us, deterministic replies are important for the assistant in our dashboard. We want to keep hallucinations low. What do you recommend?
[02:02] Priya: For deterministic behavior, temp 0.0-0.2 plus top_p ~0.9 works well. Also consider prompt engineering and system messages. We can also pin model variants — smaller models reduce cost but sometimes increase hallucination rate.
[02:19] Tom: Are there pre-configured models that Redwood recommends for chat? 
[02:23] Jordan: We curate a catalog and mark performance profiles; for high-quality chat we often recommend the 'rwd-chat-v2' family (example name) or compatible open models. We'll include the model guide in the deck.
[02:34] [02:34] Priya: Now I'll demo streaming via the SDK in Python. Code (paraphrased):
  from redwood import RedwoodClient  # pseudo
  client = RedwoodClient(api_key=...)
  with client.chat.stream(model='rwd-chat-v2', messages=msgs, temperature=0.1) as stream:
      for chunk in stream:
          print(chunk.text, end='')
[02:58] Priya: In practice the SDK yields chunks every 50-200ms depending on the model and load; that gives the UI a token-by-token feel.
[03:08] Maya: Nice — and how do you reconcile stream replays if there's a disconnect?
[03:12] Priya: Two approaches: 1) attempt resume with the same idempotency key and server-assisted replays up to a short history window; 2) if not possible, restart generation but use prompt prefix caching to warm the model so you only re-generate the tail. Our runtime supports prefix/KV cache to speed replays.
[03:29] Liam (SRE): Any guidance on concurrency and rate limits? We expect bursts.
[03:33] Jordan: Hosted has rate limits per org and per route; we expose headers for remaining quota. For bursts we suggest token buckets and client-side batching. If you need steady high throughput, Dedicated is an option.
[03:45] Tom: Ok. Show us a couple of param tradeoff examples — low latency vs cost.
[03:50] Priya: Sure. Example 1: Lower max_tokens reduces cost and latency; but if you truncate completions, you may lose context. Example 2: Increase temperature for creative responses but that can increase generation length unpredictably. Example 3: top_p can constrain randomness while still allowing non-zero temperature.
[04:12] [04:12] Priya: I'll run three calls back-to-back in the Console: streaming on, temp 0.0, max_tokens 200 — you can see tokens start streaming immediately. Next I'll change temp to 0.8 and replay to show differences in answer style.
[04:28] [04:28] (audio: faint typing)
[04:32] Priya: Here you can also enable stop sequences so the model will stop when it emits a special token — useful for structured outputs.
[04:40] Maya: Are function/tool calls supported in hosted? We plan to call internal tools.
[04:45] Jordan: Yes, hosted supports function/tool-calling patterns and structured outputs. We surface them in the SDK and Console. For PII/exec we can recommend a pattern that emits a structured JSON payload which you post-process with your own tool runner.
[04:58] Tom: About privacy: do you retain prompts/responses? Can we enable no retention?
[05:03] Jordan: By default redwood retains logs for a short period for debugging and billing, but we offer retention controls for enterprise customers and Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) for air-gapped compliance. We support KMS integrations for customer-managed keys. I'll add the SOC2 + retention doc to the follow-ups.
[05:18] Liam: Great — we need SOC2 and audit logs for our security team.
[05:22] Priya: We'll attach the security pack.
[05:24] [05:24] Jordan: Back to retries: I'll share a recommended retry policy — typically 3 attempts with exponential backoff (e.g., base 200ms, factor 2, jitter). For idempotency you use a request_id header. For generation endpoints that create nondeterministic outputs, ensure your UX handles duplicate responses appropriately.
[05:45] Maya: For chat we want exactly-once appearence in the conversation history. Any patterns?
[05:49] Priya: One approach is optimistic UI: show tentative output and then confirm when the server responds; use request IDs to de-duplicate server-side. If response replays happen, client can patch the end rather than inserting duplicates.
[06:03] Tom: Can you show the SDK retry config example?
[06:06] Priya: Sure (paraphrasing):
  client = RedwoodClient(...)
  resp = client.chat.create(..., retry_policy={"max_attempts":3, "backoff_ms":200, "jitter":true})
  # For streaming, the SDK will surface stream exceptions and helper to resume
[06:28] [06:28] Jordan: We also surface metrics in Console: per-route p50/p95 latency, token counts, and cost per generate. That helps correlate prompt changes to cost.
[06:38] Maya: Does Console show token-level cost estimates before a run?
[06:41] Priya: We show estimates based on max_tokens and model price per token. It's an estimate, but good for planning.
[06:49] Tom: About retries again: if we get 429s, can we request higher quota or burst windows?
[06:55] Jordan: Yes, we can adjust limits for committed customers. For bursts, we have burst credit and reserved capacity in Dedicated. For hosted, talk with your AE.
[07:07] [07:07] (crosstalk)
[07:10] Priya: Now I'll demo a simple end-to-end: web UI makes streaming call to the SDK, we append token chunks to the chat box, and when stream completes we call the analytics endpoint.
[07:22] Priya: Note for browser clients, we recommend a small proxy layer so you don't leak API keys; use short-lived tokens.
[07:29] Liam: Do you support SAML SSO and RBAC?
[07:33] Jordan: Yes, SSO (SAML/OIDC) and RBAC are part of enterprise offerings. We'll include that in the security packet.
[07:42] Maya: Any recommended defaults for prod chat?
[07:45] Priya: Start with temp 0.1, top_p 0.9, max_tokens tuned to your longest expected reply, use stop sequences for structured outputs, and set a reasonable retry policy. Monitor p95 latency and adjust model or Dedicated/reserved capacity if you need tighter SLOs.
[08:02] [08:02] Tom: Can we run a short perf benchmark through you? We want a baseline for 200ms target p95.
[08:08] Jordan: Yes, we can — typically we ask customers to share a prompt set and target throughput/latency and we run a quick benchmark on hosted; if you need sustained low p95 we may recommend Dedicated. We'll run a short smoke test on our side once you share the prompts.
[08:23] Priya: I'll note that as an action item.
[08:26] [08:26] Priya: Quick note on caching: prefix/KV cache can dramatically reduce latency for repeated contexts. If your product has a lot of shared context we can cache the first N tokens and only generate the tail. That reduces GPU work and cost.
[08:41] Maya: That sounds useful — our customers reuse a lot of standard instructions.
[08:45] Priya: Exactly.
[08:48] [08:48] Jordan: Any other product questions?
[08:51] Tom: A few: Do you provide SDKs in Nodejs? What's the expected maintenance window?
[08:55] Jordan: SDKs in Python, Node, and Go; we maintain semver and release notes in the repo. For hosted, we publish planned maintenance windows in Console and provide alerts for enterprise.
[09:08] Maya: How do we instrument prompts for evals and rollbacks if a new model causes regressions?
[09:14] Priya: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring tied to prompt sets and evals; we can alert on regressions and allow rollback to a pinned model. For hosted you can pin model versions per route to avoid surprise behavior.
[09:29] [09:29] Tom: Can you show an example of pinned model in config?
[09:32] Priya: Sure; in route config you set model: rwd-chat-v2@v20260201. That pins to a specific model snapshot.
[09:41] Liam: Regarding logs, do we get full transcripts in audit logs?
[09:45] Jordan: We can include full request/response logs in audit exports for enterprise, and we support redaction rules for PII. We'll share the log retention options.
[09:56] [09:56] (brief pause)
[10:00] Priya: Wrapping up with a quick live example that shows retries: I'll intentionally throttle the request to trigger a 429 and show how the SDK retries with backoff.
[10:12] [10:12] (typing, simulated 429 returned)
[10:18] Priya: You see the SDK waited ~350ms then retried, then succeeded on attempt 2. The UI shows a short spinner and then resumes streaming.
[10:27] Maya: That's helpful. Does the SDK expose hooks for custom backoff?
[10:31] Priya: Yes, you can pass a retry hook or override the policy at the call-level.
[10:37] Jordan: Ok, time check — about 10 minutes left. Any final deep technical topics?
[10:42] Tom: One last: can we do server-side caching of embeddings or completions?
[10:46] Priya: Embeddings are idempotent — cache keys can be the text + model version. For completions, deterministic settings help; caching full outputs is possible with careful keys.
[10:58] [10:58] Jordan: Great. We'll follow up with the pricing and POC plan. Priya will send the SDK notebook and the security packet. Tom will share prompts and target latency.
[11:10] Tom: Sounds good. Thanks Jordan and Priya — this was useful.
[11:14] Maya: Yes thanks.
[11:16] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll send notes and next steps.
